title: The placebo effect

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A recent experiment involved a straightforward comparison of the effectiveness of a sedative, or calming drug, and a stimulant – a drug that produces increased activity. Sixty volunteers were randomly selected to receive one compound or another. The results were clear: those given the sedative were almost twice as likely to feel drowsy as those given the stimulant. No surprise there – except that the volunteers hadn’t been given either a sedative or a stimulant. All the volunteers had received the same harmless compound, the only difference being how the pills looked – the ‘sedatives’ were a relaxing blue colour, while the ‘stimulants’ came in vibrant red. Far from demonstrating the sedative powers of a drug, the study had highlighted the astonishing power of the mind to affect the body. This is no freak finding, either. Over the years, a wealth of similar evidence has emerged for the so-called placebo – from the Latin for ‘I will please’ – effect, in which the mere belief that a therapy is beneficial can be enough to make people well.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Placebos are generally regarded by medical practitioners as ethically dubious substitutes for proper therapies, but this is actually a relatively recent attitude. Up until the early 20th century, pills made of bread dough were routinely used by physicians to convince patients to get better. Their effectiveness was regarded as entirely emotional. By the mid-20th century, however, the emergence of more scientific attitudes towards medical treatment had led to a shift in perspective. Placebos were seen as ethically justifiable only in clinical trials, where they served as the baseline against which to assess the effectiveness of unproven therapies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: But as the results from the first such trials came in, researchers were shocked to discover how many patients appeared to benefit from placebos. In 1995, American medical researcher Henry Beecher published a landmark paper entitled The Powerful Placebo, which reviewed the outcome of 15 placebo-controlled trials and concluded that the proportion of patients who improved after being given only a placebo was typically around 35 per cent. That figure has entered medical folklore. But Beecher had made a fatal blunder by assuming the placebo effect was the sole explanation for any improvement. In reality, there are a myriad of possible explanations. Many medical problems such as back pain are ‘self-limiting’, meaning they can get better of their own accord. ‘The one in three figure is a myth,’ says Irvine Kirsch, a leading expert on the placebo effect at the University of Hull, UK.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: So what is the real figure? In 2001, two Danish researchers published a study designed to reveal the true power of the placebo. Asbjorn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gotzsche examined the outcome of over 100 clinical trials where a genuine therapy had been compared to giving no treatment at all, as well as to a placebo. What Hróbjartsson and Gotzsche found still provokes controversy. Far from benefiting one in three patients, the placebo effect appeared to be medically useless.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The results made headlines around the world, the media seizing on them as proof that the placebo effect was a myth. In reality, Hróbjartsson and Gotzsche did not dispute the existence of the effect – they simply suggested that it is too small to be medically useful. But other researchers insist this goes too far, arguing that the entire study was fundamentally flawed. Most of the doubt has focused on the way the study tried to find a ‘typical’ placebo response rate by lumping together studies of everything from the common cold to Alzheimer’s disease. ‘It makes more sense to evaluate the effects of particular treatments on particular disorders,’ says Kirsch. ‘There are very strong placebo effects in the treatment of some symptoms, like pain, while there are other conditions for which placebos may not be effective at all, like diabetes.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other researchers doubt the reliability of any study of the placebo effect based on clinical trials with people who are ill. ‘The reason is very simple,’ says placebo effect researcher Fabrizio Benedetti of the University of Turin, Italy. ‘In a clinical trial, the patients know that they have only a 50 per cent chance of getting either the placebo or the active drug, so they have uncertain expectations.’ That added layer of confusion is removed in tests where healthy volunteers are told they will definitely receive an active compound, but are actually given a placebo. Such lab studies have provided compelling evidence for the reality of the placebo effect.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Other studies have focused on how the placebo effect physically affects the body. For example, Benedetti and his colleagues gave volunteers injections of capsaicin, the natural substance that produces the burning-like sensation of chilli being placed on the skin, and then handed out a cream which they said was a powerful painkiller. In reality, the cream contained no active ingredients – but the volunteers reported that it had eased their pain. The researchers then gave the volunteers naloxone, a compound that blocks the action of the body’s own painkilling compounds – and the volunteers’ pain returned. The researchers concluded that the placebo effect was bringing the body’s own painkillers to bear.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: If such potent effects can be combined with conventional therapies, the results could transform medicine. ‘Imagine being able to give a drug on Monday, a placebo on Tuesday, the drug again on Wednesday and so on,’ says Benedetti. This is no longer simply a theoretical possibility: a recent study by Benedetti has shown that the dosage of a powerful painkilling drug given to sick people following surgery could be reduced by over one-third without loss of effectiveness. Such results may herald a kinder, gentler form of medicine.

content: A substance by the name of {{22}} was administered to participants in the study. This provoked intense irritation similar to that which occurs when {{23}} comes into contact with the skin. The participants finally received a dose of a substance called {{26}} which stopped their internal painkillers from functioning. The pain then returned.

subtitle: Ever drunk a cup of coffee, felt more awake, and then been told it was decaffeinated? That is the placebo effect. Robert Matthews explores new research in this area
